getting-started.title: 🚀 Getting started
getting-started.text: 🚀 Getting started The folders it needs The plugin is developed next to the projects it uses: go.mod replaces Go Simulator, Go Renderer and Go Scene Builder with the folders beside this one, and the example starts the terrain and climate plugins from theirs. Clone them side by side: go-renderer/ go-scene-builder/ go-simulator/ go-simulator-climate/ go-simulator-terrain/ go-simulator-flora/ ← this repository Running the example cd ../go-simulator go run ./cmd/simulate -rules ../go-simulator-flora/examples/valley.yaml -output results/ examples/valley.yaml grows the vegetation of a synthetic mountain, 6 × 4 km and 1800 m high ( relieve.json and relieve.f32 next to it), from bare ground over 200 years: heather first, then oak in the lowlands and pine on the slopes. Nothing in it comes from any world. The rules file starts three plugins with go run , so nothing needs installing: plugins: - {name: terrain, command: [go, run, .], directory: ../../go-simulator-terrain} - {name: climate, command: [go, run, .], directory: ../../go-simulator-climate} - {name: flora, command: [go, run, .], directory: ..} and one stage on a yearly clock, where the relief and the climate come before the vegetation that reads them: stages: - name: valley clock: {unit: year, from: 0, to: 200, step: 1} snapshots: [50, 100, 200] snapshot_fields: [vegetation, tree_cover] rules: - rule: relief # terrain: elevation and slope - rule: climate # climate: temperature, precipitation and the biomes - rule: vegetation # this plugin: the species and the landscape's settings name: valley - rule: vegetation_indicators with: {vegetation: valley, years: [50, 100, 200]} The whole species list and every setting are in writing a scenario ; the rules file's own keys are in Go Simulator's rules file reference . What it writes cmd/simulate runs the stage to its end and saves, in the output folder: File What is in it valley 50 vegetation.f32 and .json the vegetation field at year 50: which species marks every cell (−1 for bare ground), with its grid in the .json valley 50 tree_cover.f32 and .json the share of the ground under trees in every cell valley 50.geojson the entities at year 50 (none here) events.jsonl every event: the climate's biomes , this plugin's vegetation (the names, labels, forms and heights of the species) and vegetation_indicators in the listed years The same for years 100 and 200. An indicators event looks like this (year 200 of the example): {"forest_hectares": 1085, "shrubland_hectares": 893, "grassland_hectares": 0, "bare_hectares": 154, "hectares_oak": 530.69, "hectares_heather": 562.13, "hectares_pine": 30.99, "hectares_birch": 22.38, "hectares_meadow": 0.7, "vegetation": "valley", "year": 200} Every field and event is described in the model . The tests go vet ./... go test ./... The tests run the plugin inside a Go Simulator host on synthetic landscapes and check what must hold anywhere: every species within its habitat, pioneers followed by shade-tolerant trees, disturbances keeping pioneers, anchored plants staying (and small crowns covering their share of a cell), managed land keeping forms out, soft habitat edges, and the same seed giving the same landscape.

how-it-works.title: 🔍 How it works

sections.text: How the plugin fits Go Simulator

how-it-works.text: 🔍 How it works How the plugin fits Go Simulator Go Simulator is the host. It keeps the world (its fields, events and entities) and moves the clock. The flora plugin is a separate program the host starts ( main.go serves it over standard input and output, Go Simulator's protocol ). At the start the plugin describes itself: its two rules, their parameters, what each one reads and what it writes. That description is also where the rules reference comes from. vegetation reads the temperature , precipitation , elevation , slope and biome fields, the climate's biomes event and the anchors, and writes the vegetation , tree_cover , shrub_cover and herb_cover fields (and cover_<id> when asked). Its instance name names the landscape. vegetation_indicators reads nothing from other plugins: it measures the landscape of the vegetation rule it names and emits a vegetation_indicators event. A plugin never touches the renderer: it reads its copy of the world and answers with changes (Go Simulator's writing plugins ). Fields use physical units and shapes world units, as Go Simulator's vocabulary lists. The plugin reads what the terrain and climate plugins publish from the world instead of loading it again, so they must come before it in the rules file. A step The stage's clock counts years. When the simulation starts, the vegetation rule lays the grid over the climate's extent, samples the fields, works out how well every cell suits every species, plants the anchored plants and publishes the bare landscape. On every step it simulates the years the step covers, one at a time: The seeds are spread first, for the whole landscape, with a separable Gaussian kernel (along the rows, then along the columns). Then every land cell grows, is disturbed and ages, from the state it had at the start of the year, so the cells are shared out over the processors. The fields are published again every publish_every years. The model has every formula. The code File What is in it main.go starts the plugin flora/plugin.go the two rules, setting up the landscape, anchors and regions flora/landscape.go the grid and how the world's fields are sampled on it flora/habitat.go habitats, soft edges and distances to anchors flora/species.go species, settings, managed land, disturbance flora/succession.go one year: saplings, recruitment, death, room, disturbance, light flora/dispersal.go the seed kernel and the parallel loop flora/publish.go the fields, the names and the indicators How the pictures were made The maps and charts in these pages were drawn from the plugin's own answers. A small throwaway program, kept outside the repository, ran the real plugin in a Go Simulator host and read the fields it published after every year: The example mountain (the README's picture and the charts of its indicators): examples/valley.yaml with the real terrain and climate plugins, unchanged except for publish_every: 1 and species_fields: true , so every year could be drawn. Each cell shows the species of the vegetation field, paler where it covers less, shaded by the relief. Spreading, succession, disturbance, habitat and managed land : small made-up flat fields with a stand-in for the climate that only names the biomes, and the scenarios written in the pictures' captions. The tests use the same kind of synthetic landscape. They are SVG drawings with their own light and dark colours, not screenshots: the viewer does not draw fields yet. The maps inside them are the cells of the published fields. The diagrams (how it fits, a cell, one year, the light) were drawn by hand in the same style; the cell in the landscape diagram is an example, not a measured one. The pictures of the made-up island in the model were in the docs before these pages; the scenario they come from is not in the repository.

overview.title: Welcome to Go Flora Simulator 👋

sections.text: All the pages, in reading order

overview.text: Welcome to Go Flora Simulator 👋 The flora plugin grows a simulated world's plants , year by year for centuries: grass first, then shrubs, then pioneer trees, and in the end the forest that fits each place. Every species is a card of traits (how tall, how long it lives, how far its seeds fly, where it can live). The plugin lets them spread, compete for light and room, and recover from storms, on the ground and weather the other plugins give it. Is it for me? ✅ You use Go Simulator and want plants that grow over centuries . ✅ You want to set it up by writing a rules file : no programming needed. ✅ You are curious about the science behind it: the pages explain the model with pictures. Where to start Pick the line that sounds like you. If you… Read Time are new and want to see it work 🏴‍☠️ The quest : two hundred years of an island's plants, in 5 levels 45 min want to run its example Getting started 10 min want to write species of your own Writing a scenario 15 min are looking up a parameter Rules reference — All the pages, in reading order The menu on the left (or the files in docs/ ) follows this order. Start Overview : this page The quest Getting started Understand Writing a scenario The model How it works Reference Rules reference 🚧 Not done yet Plants do not react yet to other plugins' entities: a growing city does not clear the forest, and abandoned fields do not grow back. Pictures of the 3D viewer itself: the viewer does not draw fields yet, so the pictures in these pages are 2D drawings of the fields the plugin published, not screenshots (see how the pictures were made ). Seasons (flowering, leaves) belong to the climate's seasons rule, not to this plugin. Words you will meet Word What it means Terminal The window where you type commands: Terminal on macOS and Linux, PowerShell on Windows. Repository A project's folder of files, kept on GitHub. git clone <address> copies it to your computer. Plugin A small program that adds one ability to another: here, one kind of simulation each. Rules file A text file (YAML) that says which plugins to use, with which numbers, for how long: no programming needed. Field A grid of numbers laid over the world: the height of every spot, its temperature, its rain. Quest The tutorial of these docs: short levels, each ending with something that works and an achievement. The family Go Flora Simulator is one of a family of small projects that work together: Project What it does Go Renderer draws 3D scenes and flat interfaces Go UI buttons, panels and whole applications Go UI for Android Android apps that look like Android's own Go Sound sound and music Go Scene Builder 3D scenes from a flat map Go Simulator simulations that change a scene Go Terrain Simulator ground shaped by rivers Go Climate Simulator weather and biomes Go Flora Simulator (this one) forests that grow Go Urban Simulator towns that grow Go Motion Simulator a scene that moves Go for 3DS Go on the Nintendo 3DS ⚠️ All of them are educational experiments , written with an AI assistant and pending review by their author: good for learning and playing, not for production.

rules-reference.title: 📏 Rules of the flora plugin
rules-reference.text: 📏 Rules of the flora plugin Version 0.1.0, protocol 2. Vegetation that spreads, competes for light, ages and comes back after disturbances, year by year, where the climate and the relief suit each species (after LANDIS: Mladenoff and He 1999; Scheller et al. 2007). This reference is generated from what the plugin itself tells the host (the describe message), so it always matches the code. Parameters go under with: in a rules file; see Go Simulator's rules file reference . Rule What it does vegetation Sets up the landscape from the world's climate and relief, and advances its vegetation every step. Its instance name names the landscape. vegetation_indicators Emits a "vegetation_indicators" event in the listed years (every step when none): hectares of every species, of forest, shrubland, grassland and bare ground, and every region's forest share and commonest species. vegetation Sets up the landscape from the world's climate and relief, and advances its vegetation every step. Its instance name names the landscape. Reads: entities with property anchor ; fields temperature , precipitation , elevation , slope , biome ; events biomes Writes: vegetation , tree_cover , shrub_cover , herb_cover Parameter Type Default Meaning species list [{id, name, form: tree | shrub | herb, height, longevity, maturity, shade_tolerance, dispersal, growth, habitat, spreads}] cell number km between cell centres (default: the temperature field's) softness map {temperature: °C, precipitation: mm, elevation: m, slope, distance: m}: how far a habitat fades past its edges disturbance map {chance: per cell and year, severity: share of trees and shrubs lost} background_seeds number 0 seeds reaching every cell from far away publish_every number 10 years between publishing the fields species_fields boolean false also publish cover_ for every species managed list [{where: condition over the cell's facts, forms: [herb…]}]: land people keep, where only those forms grow metres_per_unit number 1000 size of a world unit in metres (the scenes are in km) seed number 1 the same seed gives the same landscape vegetation_indicators Emits a "vegetation_indicators" event in the listed years (every step when none): hectares of every species, of forest, shrubland, grassland and bare ground, and every region's forest share and commonest species. Reads: nothing from other plugins Writes: nothing (it only emits events) Parameter Type Default Meaning vegetation text instance name of the vegetation rule years list

the-model.title: 🌳 The flora model
the-model.text: 🌳 The flora model Forests do not appear all at once. On bare ground, grasses and gorse arrive first; then trees that love the sun, like birch and pine; and, slowly, under their shade, the trees that can wait in the dark take over. A storm or a fire opens a clearing and the story starts again there. The flora plugin plays that story, year by year, for every species you give it, wherever the climate and the land let it live. It knows nothing about any world: the species, their traits and their habitats come from the scenario . This page explains what happens in each cell, every year. The pictures on this page come from real runs of the plugin, drawn in 2D from the fields it published: the example mountain, and small made-up fields that show one thing each ( how they were made ). The landscape The landscape is a grid over the climate's extent, with cells of cell km (default: the temperature field's). At the start the plugin samples, at every cell centre, the fields of the world: temperature and precipitation (from the climate plugin), elevation and slope (from the terrain plugin) bilinearly, and biome by the nearest cell. Land is every cell with a biome (or above sea level when there is no biome field). The names of the biomes come from the climate's biomes event. In every land cell, every species has: its cover : the share of the ground its plants take, 0 to 1; its saplings : the share of the ground with young plants waiting for room (the advance regeneration of LANDIS); how many years it has grown there, which decides when it bears seeds. Habitat A species' habitat is an envelope over the facts of a cell (bioclimatic envelope models, Busby 1991), written like Go Simulator's conditions : habitat: temperature: {min: 9, max: 18} # °C, the yearly mean precipitation: {min: 900} # mm a year elevation: {max: 1500} # metres slope: {max: 0.8} # rise over run biome: [riverbank] # one of the climate's biomes distance_to_old_oak: {max: 60} # metres from an anchor of the rules file Inside every range the habitat suits the species fully. Past an edge it fades linearly to nothing over the fact's softness ( softness: {temperature: 1.5, precipitation: 150, slope: 0.1, distance: 40} , in each fact's unit; without one, the edge is hard). Values that are not ranges hold or not. The suitability of a cell is the product of every fact's: 1 where everything suits, 0 where anything is out of reach. It is worked out once, at the start. A made-up strip from 16 °C in the west to 0 °C in the east. Each tree grows where its range is; a plant dies faster where the habitat suits it only in part, so where two ranges meet only at their soft edges neither tree closes the forest, and the meadow keeps the gap. Layers and light Light is what plants compete for. Every species has a form: tree , shrub or herb . Trees shade shrubs, shrubs shade herbs. The light that reaches a layer through the layers above it is 1 − 0.9 × min(1, their cover) . A species needs light by its shade tolerance (1 to 5): need = (5 − tolerance) / 4 × 0.8 , so tolerance 5 grows in deep shade and tolerance 1 needs 80 % of full light. With some light it keeps (light − need) / (1 − need) of its growth, none below what it needs. One year This is the heart of the model. For every land cell and species, from the state at the start of the year: Seeds. Mature plants (grown at least maturity years in the cell) spread seeds around them with a Gaussian kernel as wide as their dispersal (metres); background_seeds reach every cell from far away (birds, storms). Species with spreads: false never seed. Saplings. Seeds become saplings where the habitat suits the species and there is light for them, both in the gaps of their layer and under its plants: in the gaps, with the light the taller layers leave, less the shade of the plants around the gap: tall trees shade a small gap (0.6 when their layer is closed), shrubs less (0.3), grasses not at all; the ground a disturbance cleared gets nearly full light; under the plants of their own layer, with the light that reaches the ground. saplings += growth × seeds × suitability × (light in gaps + light under plants) × (1 − saplings) ; then 10 % of the saplings die waiting, more where the habitat does not suit. Recruitment. Saplings take the room plants left in their layer: recruited = min(saplings, growth × saplings × room × suitability × light from above) . Death. Plants die of age ( 1 / longevity a year), of a habitat that does not suit them (up to 20 % a year) and of shade too deep for them (up to 10 % a year). Room. If the species of a layer together grew past the ground there is, they share it out in proportion. Disturbance. With disturbance.chance a year, a cell loses severity of its trees and shrubs (windthrow, fire) and they start again; herbs and saplings stay. How a forest spreads Seeds only come from mature plants, and they land around them as far as the species' dispersal . Every plant that grows from them bears seeds in its turn once it is mature, so a species advances as a front, faster the farther its seeds fly and the sooner it matures. Birch (dispersal 400 m, seeds from year 8) against oak (60 m, from year 40), from one planted tree each, with no seeds from far away. Birch, which needs full light, only fills about a third of the ground: it regenerates only where its own cover leaves enough light. Succession So pioneers that need full light take open ground first and cannot follow themselves under their own shade, while shade-tolerant species waiting below take over as the pioneers age: succession. Frequent disturbances keep the pioneers in the landscape; rare ones let the tolerant species close the forest. A light-demanding species forms open woodland, because it only regenerates where its own cover leaves enough light. A made-up field where every species could live everywhere, from bare ground and without disturbances: meadow, then birch, then oak; beech, the most shade-tolerant and slowest, is still spreading at year 400. The same story on a larger made-up island, with more species: The example island at years 30, 80, 140 and 200: shrubs first, then pine on the mountain and oak in the lowlands Share of the island under forest, shrubs, grass and bare ground over 200 years The example island from bare ground: grassland, then a long time of shrubland, and finally the forest closes after about 150 years. Disturbance Every year each cell has disturbance.chance of losing severity (default 0.8) of its trees and shrubs, as after windthrow or a fire. The cleared ground gets nearly full light, so the pioneers come back there first. The field of the succession chart at year 400 with three disturbance chances. With a gap every 200 years in a cell the oak still holds the forest; with one every 50 years, birch and meadow mark most of it. Anchors Anchors of the rules file take part in two ways: Plants ( role: plant , properties: {species, crown} ): a fixed plant, such as an old tree the story names. Its species covers the cells within crown metres of it or, when the crown is smaller than a cell, the share of the cell under it; the other species of its layer make room. It is mature from the start and stays every year. Regions ( role: region , an outline): areas the indicators measure. Any anchor can be used in habitats as distance_to_<anchor id> , in metres, for plants that grow near something. Managed land Land people keep, such as fields and orchards: where its condition holds (written like a habitat, without soft edges), only the listed forms grow. managed: - {where: {biome: [fields]}, forms: [herb]} - {where: {distance_to_old_oak: {max: 120}}, forms: [herb]} # a clearing round a tree The two managed lands above on a made-up field of 2.4 × 1.4 km in cells of 20 m, with an anchor that plants an old oak: herbs keep the fields and the clearing, and the forest closes everywhere else. What it publishes Output When Content event vegetation start names , labels , forms , heights of the species field vegetation start and every publish_every years the species that most marks every cell: the commonest tree where tree cover reaches 0.3, else the commonest shrub where shrubs reach 0.3, else the commonest herb where herbs reach 0.2; −1 for bare ground fields tree_cover , shrub_cover , herb_cover the same share of the ground under each layer fields cover_<id> the same, with species_fields: true cover of every species event vegetation_indicators the listed years hectares of every species; hectares of forest, shrubland, grassland and bare ground; for every region, its forest share and its commonest species Put the stage's snapshots at multiples of publish_every , and keep only the fields worth saving with snapshot_fields : a large landscape's fields take megabytes each. Determinism and speed The same seed gives the same landscape: the chance of a disturbance comes from a hash of the seed, the year and the cell, so cells can be worked on in parallel in any order. Cells are spread over the processors. A landscape of about 700,000 land cells and 18 species takes about a third of a second a year. Known limits Plants do not react yet to other plugins' entities: a growing city does not clear the forest, and abandoned fields do not grow back. The viewer does not draw fields yet; Go Scene Builder can sow the vegetation from the vegetation field as a layer, as it does with biomes. Seasons (flowering, leaves) belong to the climate's seasons rule. Tests go test ./... The tests grow synthetic landscapes and check what must hold anywhere: every species within its habitat, pioneers followed by shade-tolerant trees, disturbances keeping pioneers, anchored plants staying (and small crowns covering their share of a cell), managed land keeping forms out, soft habitat edges, and the same seed giving the same landscape.

the-quest.title: The flora quest

sections.text: Final challenge · Keeper of the old oak

the-quest.text: The flora quest Grow an island's plants from bare ground over two hundred years, one level at a time. Each level teaches one piece of the flora plugin and ends with the island's vegetation in 3D. The quest map: a road from START through 5 levels — Sower, Heathkeeper, Pioneer, Patient forester and Storm warden — to a final challenge, Keeper of the old oak We use the mountain island of the terrain quest and the weather of the climate quest . Grass comes first, then heather, then birches, and over the centuries pine takes the heights and oak the wet slopes; storms open gaps; and an old oak the story names stands in its clearing. Every level has the same shape: the idea (explained with something from everyday life), the rules , a checkpoint to know it works, and an optional bonus . Before you start You need Go 1.25 and GEOS ( sudo apt install libgeos-dev , brew install geos ). Clone the projects side by side, and make a folder for the quest: git clone https://github.com/akrck02/go-renderer git clone https://github.com/akrck02/go-scene-builder git clone https://github.com/akrck02/go-simulator git clone https://github.com/akrck02/go-simulator-terrain git clone https://github.com/akrck02/go-simulator-climate git clone https://github.com/akrck02/go-simulator-flora mkdir woods && cd woods go mod init example.com/woods Put the island's relief in it as island.json and island.f32 (the terrain quest's end snapshot, renamed), and empty.geojson , a map with nothing on it: {"type": "FeatureCollection", "properties": {"units": "km"}, "features": []} Looking at the vegetation The plugin publishes a field vegetation : for every cell, the species that marks it most (or −1, bare ground). layer/main.go turns a snapshot of it into a layer Go Scene Builder can colour and sow trees on: // Command layer turns a snapshot of the vegetation field into a layer go-scene-builder colours and // sows: the species' names, from the run's events, become the layer's labels, and bare ground // (−1 in the field) becomes a label of its own, "bare". // // go run ./layer results "island 200" vegetation.json package main import ( "bufio" "encoding/binary" "encoding/json" "log" "os" "path/filepath" "strings" ) func main() { folder, snapshot, out := os.Args[1], os.Args[2], os.Args[3] names := speciesNames(filepath.Join(folder, "events.jsonl")) var header map[string]any content, err := os.ReadFile(filepath.Join(folder, snapshot+" vegetation.json")) if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } if err := json.Unmarshal(content, &header); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } values, err := os.ReadFile(filepath.Join(folder, snapshot+" vegetation.f32")) if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } cells := make([]float32, len(values)/4) if err := binary.Read(strings.NewReader(string(values)), binary.LittleEndian, cells); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } for index, value := range cells { if value < 0 { cells[index] = float32(len(names)) // bare ground: the label after the species } } header["labels"] = append(names, "bare") written, _ := json.Marshal(header) if err := os.WriteFile(out, written, 0o644); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } file, err := os.Create(strings.TrimSuffix(out, ".json") + ".f32") if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } defer file.Close() if err := binary.Write(file, binary.LittleEndian, cells); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } } // speciesNames reads the names of the species from the vegetation event at the start of the run. func speciesNames(path string) []string { file, err := os.Open(path) if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } defer file.Close() lines := bufio.NewScanner(file) lines.Buffer(make([]byte, 1<<20), 1<<24) for lines.Scan() { var event struct { Name string `json:"name"` Data struct { Names []string `json:"names"` } `json:"data"` } if json.Unmarshal(lines.Bytes(), &event) == nil && event.Name == "vegetation" { return event.Data.Names } } log.Fatal("no vegetation event in ", path) return nil } models.yaml , the trees (Go Scene Builder's models ): models: fir: variants: 3 vary: {color: 0.1, scale: [0.8, 1.3]} parts: - {shape: cylinder, radius: 0.3, height: 2, color: "#5a4632"} - {shape: cone, radius: 2.2, height: 9, at: [0, 1.5, 0], color: "#2f4a2c", material: {foliage: true}, move: 0.2, grow: 0.15} oak: variants: 3 vary: {color: 0.12, warmth: 0.06, scale: [0.8, 1.25]} parts: - {shape: cylinder, radius: 0.35, top_radius: 0.25, height: 3, color: "#5a4632"} - {shape: blob, size: [6, 5, 6], at: [0, 5, 0], wobble: 0.15, move: 0.6, grow: 0.2, color: "#56713a", material: {foliage: true}} birch: variants: 3 vary: {color: 0.1, scale: [0.8, 1.2]} parts: - {shape: cylinder, radius: 0.2, height: 4, color: "#e8e4dc"} - {shape: blob, size: [3.5, 6, 3.5], at: [0, 6, 0], wobble: 0.2, move: 0.4, grow: 0.2, color: "#8fae4a", material: {foliage: true}} view.yaml , a colour for every species and trees where trees grow: units: m chunk: 2 models: [models.yaml] environment: {sun: [250, 25], water_level: 0} terrain: color: "#8a8674" biomes: bare: {color: "#8a8674"} meadow: {color: "#a7b46a"} heather: {color: "#8c6d86"} birch: {color: "#8fa35a", decorate: [{recipe: scatter, density: 0.0015, models: {birch: 1}}]} pine: {color: "#4f6b3a", decorate: [{recipe: scatter, density: 0.002, models: {fir: 1}}]} oak: {color: "#56713a", decorate: [{recipe: scatter, density: 0.0015, models: {oak: 1}}]} old_oak: {color: "#2f4a22", decorate: [{recipe: scatter, density: 0.0001, models: {oak: 1}, scale: [3, 3]}]} After every run, for the snapshot of year 200: go run ./layer results "island 200" vegetation.json go run ../go-scene-builder/cmd/build-scene -map empty.geojson -relief island.json -layer biome=vegetation.json -style view.yaml -out woods.glb go run ../go-renderer/cmd/visor woods.glb The pictures were taken with -zoom 0.75 . Level 1 · The Sower Mission Pieces Time Grass over the whole island three plugins in a row, the vegetation rule, a species 8 min The idea Plants need ground and weather, and other plugins know those. So three plugins work like a relay : terrain hands the ground to climate, climate hands temperature and rain to flora. They run in the order of the stage's rules, and none knows the others: they only read the world . A species is a card of traits: what it is ( form : tree, shrub or herb), how tall, how long it lives, how soon it seeds, how far its seeds fly, and where it can live ( habitat ). Build it rules.yaml : plugins: - {name: terrain, command: [go, run, .], directory: ../go-simulator-terrain} - {name: climate, command: [go, run, .], directory: ../go-simulator-climate} - {name: flora, command: [go, run, .], directory: ../go-simulator-flora} stages: - name: island clock: {unit: year, from: 0, to: 200, step: 1} snapshots: [20, 50, 100, 200] snapshot_fields: [vegetation, tree_cover] rules: - rule: relief with: {path: island.json, origin: [0, 0]} - rule: climate with: cell: 0.1 temperature: {sea_level: 12, lapse: 6.5} rain: {wind_from: 270, background: 450, orographic: 1400} biomes: - {biome: rock, when: {slope: {min: 0.6}}} - {biome: land} - rule: vegetation name: island with: background_seeds: 0.002 disturbance: {chance: 0.004} softness: {temperature: 1.5, slope: 0.1} publish_every: 10 species: - {id: meadow, name: Meadow, form: herb, height: 0.4, longevity: 20, maturity: 1, shade_tolerance: 2, dispersal: 300, growth: 0.6, habitat: {temperature: {min: -3}}} - rule: vegetation_indicators with: {vegetation: island, years: [20, 50, 100, 200]} background_seeds lets a few seeds reach every cell from far away, so bare ground does not wait for its neighbours. go run ../go-simulator/cmd/simulate -rules rules.yaml -output results/ Checkpoint A run of 200 years takes about a second. Look at year 50: green meadow everywhere but the bare cliffs. Level 1: meadow over the whole island Achievement unlocked: Sower Learn more: Writing a scenario · The model Level 2 · The Heathkeeper Mission Pieces Time Heather that crowds the grass out a shrub, light and room 5 min The idea Plants in a cell share it like seats on a bus : there is only so much room, and taller ones shade the shorter. A shrub over the grass takes its light, and only grass that bears shade keeps a seat. Heather is taller than meadow grass and lives longer. Build it Add to species : - {id: heather, name: Heather, form: shrub, height: 1, longevity: 40, maturity: 3, shade_tolerance: 2, dispersal: 100, growth: 0.3, habitat: {temperature: {min: -1}}} Checkpoint By year 50 heather (purple) covers most of the island; meadow keeps a few patches. Level 2: purple heather over most of the island Achievement unlocked: Heathkeeper Level 3 · The Pioneer Mission Pieces Time The first trees a tree, its habitat, dispersal 5 min The idea Birch is a pioneer : the first settler of a new town, quick to arrive, quick to build, but not staying long. It seeds young and its seeds fly far (400 m), but it needs full light ( shade_tolerance: 1 ) and lives only 90 years. Build it - {id: birch, name: Birch, form: tree, height: 18, longevity: 90, maturity: 8, shade_tolerance: 1, dispersal: 400, growth: 0.35, habitat: {temperature: {min: 0, max: 10}, biome: [land]}} Its habitat keeps it between 0 and 10 °C and off the rock biome. Checkpoint By year 50, birch wood rises on the cooler upper slopes, its trees standing on the scene. Level 3: a birch wood on the upper slopes, heather round it Achievement unlocked: Pioneer Level 4 · The Patient forester Mission Pieces Time Succession: who comes after the pioneers shade tolerance, longevity, maturity 8 min The idea Forests change hands like shifts at a lighthouse : the pioneers hold it first, but the patient ones take over. Pine bears more shade than birch and lives 250 years; oak bears more still, lives 500, but takes 40 years to seed and its acorns fall close (60 m). Slow to arrive, it wins in the end where it is warm and wet enough. This is succession . Build it - {id: pine, name: Pine, form: tree, height: 25, longevity: 250, maturity: 15, shade_tolerance: 2, dispersal: 150, growth: 0.25, habitat: {temperature: {min: 0, max: 7}, biome: [land]}} - {id: oak, name: Oak, form: tree, height: 25, longevity: 500, maturity: 40, shade_tolerance: 3, dispersal: 60, growth: 0.12, habitat: {temperature: {min: 6}, precipitation: {min: 1200}, biome: [land]}} Look at years 50, 100 and 200. Checkpoint Year 50: birch and heather. Year 100: pine darkens the summit. Year 200: oak closes the forest on the wet slopes, and heather holds only the dry edges. Level 4 at year 50: birch and heather Level 4 at year 100: pine on the summit Level 4 at year 200: oak forest over the slopes Bonus (optional): a beech that waits in the shade Achievement unlocked: Patient forester Learn more: Choosing traits Level 5 · The Storm warden Mission Pieces Time Gaps where trees fall, and the forest in numbers disturbance , vegetation_indicators 6 min The idea A storm knocks trees down, and in the gap the pioneers start again: a forest is never one age. disturbance.chance is the chance a year that a cell is hit; severity the share of trees and shrubs it takes. To know how much forest there is, the indicators rule counts hectares at the years you ask, as an event. Build it disturbance: {chance: 0.03, severity: 0.9} Checkpoint Year 200 is patchy: oak and pine broken by heather and birch where storms opened gaps. In results/events.jsonl , the vegetation_indicators event of year 200 counts the hectares of every species and of forest, shrubland, grassland and bare ground. Level 5: a forest broken into patches by storms Bonus (optional): check it An objective that fails if the storms leave less than 400 hectares of forest at year 200 (without storms, level 4 had about 1,400; with them, about 460). Achievement unlocked: Storm warden Final challenge · Keeper of the old oak The story says an old oak stands in the north-west of the island, in a clearing people keep open round it; and the low ground by the shore is fields , kept as grass. Hint: an anchor with role: plant plants a fixed tree of a species that does not spread ( spreads: false ). managed land keeps only some forms where its condition holds, and an anchor can be named in a condition as distance_to_<id> . Try it on your own first, then compare with the solution. The final challenge: the island at year 200, with meadow kept on the low ground Close up: the old oak in its clearing on the north-west slope Rare achievement unlocked: Keeper of the old oak Well done All six achievements: Sower, Heathkeeper, Pioneer, Patient forester, Storm warden and Keeper of the old oak You grew two centuries of vegetation from the laws of light, room and seed, on an island whose ground and weather were simulated by two other plugins. Ideas to keep going Idea Difficulty Hint A field per species ⭐ species_fields: true publishes cover_<id> A region measured on its own ⭐⭐ An anchor with role: region and an outline: the indicators report it A town in the clearing ⭐⭐⭐ The urban plugin Troubleshooting You see Why, and what to do no vegetation event from layer The run did not reach the flora plugin: look at the errors simulate printed Everything is bare No species' habitat fits the island: snapshot temperature from the climate and compare The trees are dots You are far away: -zoom 0.15 and -look-at x,z in the viewer unknown species for an anchor The anchor's species must be the id of a species in the list ← All the documentation

writing-a-scenario.title: 📝 Writing a scenario
writing-a-scenario.text: 📝 Writing a scenario The scenario is the with: of the vegetation rule, or a file it includes ( with: {include: vegetation.yaml} ). It names the species and the landscape's settings. cell: 0.1 # km between cell centres (default: the temperature field's) seed: 4 background_seeds: 0.002 # seeds reaching every cell from far away disturbance: {chance: 0.004, severity: 0.8} # a gap every 250 years in each cell, on average softness: {temperature: 1.5, precipitation: 150, slope: 0.1, distance: 40} publish_every: 10 # years between publishing the fields managed: - {where: {biome: [fields]}, forms: [herb]} species: - id: birch # names fields and indicators: no spaces or slashes name: Downy birch (Betula pubescens) form: tree # tree, shrub or herb height: 18 # metres, for the scene longevity: 90 # years a plant lives maturity: 8 # years before it bears seeds shade_tolerance: 1 # 1: needs full light … 5: grows in deep shade dispersal: 400 # metres its seeds usually travel growth: 0.35 # share of the free room it fills in a year habitat: {temperature: {min: 2, max: 11}, slope: {max: 0.6}} - id: beech name: Beech (Fagus sylvatica) form: tree height: 30 longevity: 300 maturity: 50 shade_tolerance: 5 dispersal: 40 growth: 0.08 habitat: {temperature: {min: 6, max: 11}, precipitation: {min: 1200}, slope: {max: 0.6}} - id: meadow name: Meadow grasses form: herb height: 0.5 longevity: 20 # perennial grasses live for decades as clumps maturity: 1 shade_tolerance: 2 dispersal: 300 growth: 0.6 habitat: {temperature: {min: 0}} - id: old_oak name: The old oak form: tree height: 20 longevity: 2000 maturity: 50 shade_tolerance: 3 dispersal: 0 growth: 0.1 spreads: false # only where an anchor plants it habitat: {} And in the rules file, the anchor that plants the old oak: anchors: - {id: old_oak, role: plant, at: [1.05, 0.55], properties: {species: old_oak, crown: 20}} An anchored old oak with managed land round it, on a made-up field: see anchors and managed land . Choosing traits The traits follow the species attributes of the LANDIS literature. Some guidance: Kind of species Shade tolerance Longevity Maturity Dispersal Growth Pioneer tree (birch, aspen) 1 60–120 5–10 200–500 m 0.3–0.4 Light-demanding conifer (pine) 2 150–300 10–20 100–200 m 0.2–0.3 Mid-tolerant broadleaf (oak) 3 300–600 25–50 30–100 m (acorns) 0.1–0.15 Shade-tolerant (beech, fir) 5 250–450 30–60 30–60 m 0.05–0.1 Shrub (heather, gorse) 1–3 20–80 3–5 50–150 m 0.25–0.4 Grass or herb 1–2 10–30 1–2 100–300 m 0.4–0.6 A forest closes in 150–250 years from bare ground; shade-tolerant trees need longer. background_seeds around 0.001–0.005 lets every species appear wherever it suits, slowly. A disturbance chance of 0.002–0.01 a year gives landscapes from closed forest to a mosaic of pioneers and late species. The succession and disturbance pictures show what these numbers do on a made-up field. Give real species habitats from their real climate (yearly mean temperature and rain), then soften the edges a little so the ranges blend.
